title: A Tale of Two Mogadishus
gist: Mogadishu's visible security gains against al-Shabaab are read by the Somali government as a durable turnaround and by opposition and civil-society voices as a fragile, elite-centered lull, and the gap matters now because the U.S. and AUSSOM's external support props are being withdrawn simultaneously.

themes.theme: The Interpretive Gap Over Mogadishu's Security

insights.claim: Al-Shabaab has not carried out a major attack in Mogadishu since mid-December 2025, a rare sustained lull in violence in the Somali capital.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A genuine, sustained drop in capital-city attacks is the empirical anchor both competing narratives are built on.
insights.quote: Al-Shabaab has not carried out a major attack in Mogadishu since mid-December 2025, a rare lull in violence in the capital of Somalia from al-Qaeda’s affiliate in the region.
insights.locator: opening paragraph

insights.claim: Government officials and opposition-aligned figures interpret the same set of facts about Mogadishu's security very differently, with one side seeing a durable turnaround and the other an elite-centered tinderbox.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Investors and policymakers relying on either narrative alone risk missing the underlying political fragility driving the outcome.
insights.quote: Both stories are built from real observations, but the two sides interpret these same facts as evidence of very different trends.
insights.locator: On a recent trip to Mogadishu

themes.theme: The Government's Case: A City That Turned the Corner

insights.claim: Somali security officials describe a purpose-built system to defeat al-Shabaab's vehicle-borne explosive device attacks, including citywide camera coverage, national-ID-linked vehicle registration, and a blacklist system requiring checkpoint searches of flagged vehicles.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Shows a concrete, technically specific counter-VBIED apparatus officials credit for the attack lull, rather than a vague claim of improved security.
insights.quote: Cameras now cover much of the city, especially its roads and businesses.
insights.locator: They describe, with evident pride

insights.claim: Somali officials say al-Shabaab's in-city 'taxation' extortion networks, a key funding source for the group, have been broken, and that U.S. airstrikes are keeping the group unable to plan.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: If true, this would cut off a core revenue stream for the insurgency; the opposition account directly disputes it.
insights.quote: al-Shabaab’s “taxation” networks inside the city—a critical source of funding for the group—have been broken
insights.locator: They also maintain

insights.claim: Officials point to new apartment-tower construction in downtown Mogadishu as evidence that investors believe the improved security will hold, and expect it to eventually ease the city's high rents.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Private construction investment is being used as an informal market signal of confidence in Somalia's security trajectory.
insights.quote: investors would not finance unless they believed the security would hold
insights.locator: They point to construction

insights.claim: A visibly loosened social scene in Mogadishu, including busier cafes, more crowded beaches, and young Somalis posting outings on TikTok without hesitation, is cited by officials as a sign fear has receded.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A soft, everyday-life indicator officials use to argue security gains are being felt by ordinary residents, not just on paper.
insights.quote: young Somalis post their outings on TikTok without a second thought
insights.locator: They point to a social scene

insights.claim: Many Somali officials believe their forces are ready to operate without the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia, particularly given Turkey's continued military backing.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: This confidence underlies Mogadishu's tolerance for AUSSOM's funding being cut off, a bet the opposition camp thinks is premature.
insights.locator: Officials extend the same confidence outward

insights.claim: President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud has announced a 'final offensive' against al-Shabaab in the coming months while proceeding unchanged with his one-person-one-vote electoral overhaul and treating his contested one-year term extension as settled.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A high-stakes military and political gamble that, if it fails, would validate the opposition's warnings about overconfidence.
insights.quote: announced a “final offensive” against al-Shabaab in the coming months
insights.locator: This has all emboldened the president

insights.claim: Opposition-aligned officials and analysts argue al-Shabaab's reduced attack tempo reflects strategic patience rather than defeat, having shifted from indiscriminate civilian violence toward fewer, higher-value attacks on government targets.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Reframes the headline 'lull' as tactical adaptation rather than degradation, implying the insurgency retains capability.
insights.quote: But they insist the group is simply playing a longer and more patient game, as it has before.
insights.locator: Rather than reading the reduced attack tempo

insights.claim: Despite government claims the networks were dismantled, al-Shabaab is reportedly still quietly collecting some taxes in Mogadishu and tracking non-payers for a later reckoning.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Directly contradicts the government's claim that al-Shabaab's funding networks in the capital have been broken.
insights.quote: the group is still quietly collecting some taxes in Mogadishu, and tracking who fails to pay for a later reckoning
insights.locator: Meanwhile, the group is still quietly collecting

insights.claim: Critics say President Hassan Sheikh's announced 'final offensive' lacks a real operational plan or a strategy for holding territory once cleared, the same gap that undid previous offensives against al-Shabaab.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Suggests the announced offensive could repeat past failures rather than deliver the decisive win the government is projecting.
insights.quote: there is no real operational plan behind the announcement, and certainly no strategy for what happens after territory is cleared
insights.locator: Officials in this camp say

insights.claim: Government demolitions clearing space for new Mogadishu construction have displaced poorer residents who cannot afford the new apartments, fueling a growing haves-versus-have-nots divide.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The construction boom the government touts as proof of confidence is, in this account, also a source of social grievance that could destabilize the calm.
insights.locator: Government demolitions clearing space

insights.claim: Opposition figures describe President Hassan Sheikh as increasingly authoritarian and governing through a narrow, hard-to-reach circle of advisers, propped up by opaque agreements with Turkey, with some invoking Siad Barre, the military dictator whose 1991 ouster triggered Somalia's civil war, as a comparison.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A comparison to Barre signals how seriously some Somalis view the risk of democratic backsliding tied to the president's consolidation of power.
insights.quote: some even invoking Siad Barre as a comparison
insights.locator: It describes the one-person-one-vote push

insights.claim: Federal member states Puntland and Jubaland have effectively withdrawn from Somalia's federal government and now operate independently of it.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Undercuts the government narrative of national consolidation even as Mogadishu itself appears calmer.
insights.quote: Federal member states Puntland and Jubaland have effectively withdrawn from the federal government and now operate independently of it.
insights.locator: Beyond the capital

insights.claim: South West State's attempted withdrawal from the federal government in March triggered months of fighting between federal-backed forces and loyalists of the ousted president, culminating in a disputed inauguration in July.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A concrete, recent instance of the center-periphery conflict that the opposition says the government's rosy narrative ignores.
insights.locator: South West State attempted the same in March

insights.claim: Somaliland has secured diplomatic recognition from Israel, making it the first country to legitimize Somaliland's independence.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A geopolitical shift that further complicates Somalia's territorial integrity narrative and could reshape regional alignments.
insights.quote: Somaliland has secured recognition from Israel, the first country to legitimate its independence.
insights.locator: Beyond the capital

insights.claim: Ugandan troops within the African Union force continue to play an indispensable role, including securing Mogadishu's airport, a function Somali forces cannot easily replace even as officials say they no longer need the mission.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Highlights a concrete operational dependency that undercuts confidence Somali forces can fully replace AUSSOM.
insights.locator: the African Union force that the government insists it no longer needs

themes.theme: External Support Is Being Withdrawn at a Fragile Moment

insights.claim: On July 1, the United States notified the African Union it would block renewal of the UN Support Office in Somalia, which provides critical logistical and operational support for AUSSOM, citing Somalia's failure to sustain security gains and internal political infighting.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Removes the financial and logistical floor under the African Union force at exactly the moment the mission's funding is already strained.
insights.quote: the United States notified the African Union that it would block renewal of United Nations Support Office in Somalia, which provides critical logistical and operational support for AUSSOM
insights.locator: In a July 1 diplomatic note

insights.claim: Even as it moves to block AUSSOM funding renewal, having already blocked a UN resolution to fund the mission late last year, the U.S. is simultaneously waging its most intensive air campaign in Somalia's history, at a pace exceeding last year's record.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A contradictory U.S. posture — escalating unilateral military strikes while defunding multilateral logistical support — that the author argues doubles down on security tactics while neglecting political strategy.
insights.quote: Even as it kneecaps AUSSOM, it has waged the most intensive air campaign in Somalia’s history, striking al-Shabaab at a pace to exceed last year’s record.
insights.locator: The move comes after the United States blocked

insights.claim: The United States currently has no ambassador in Mogadishu, and the UN special representative position, previously held by a U.S. ambassador, sits vacant, leaving no one positioned to mediate Somalia's internal political rift as external support is withdrawn.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A diplomatic vacuum at precisely the moment international mediation capacity is most needed to prevent political collapse.
insights.quote: The United States has no ambassador in Mogadishu, and the UN special representative position, last occupied by a U.S. ambassador, is sitting vacant.
insights.locator: This is compounded by an international community

themes.theme: The Author's Thesis: Political Dysfunction, Not Security, Is the Real Gap

insights.claim: Al-Shabaab has survived every past campaign against it not because it is unbeatable, but because it has never had to face a unified Somali opponent sustained over time, since political infighting repeatedly diverts government attention and gives the group room to regroup.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Reframes the core threat to Somali stability as political rather than purely military, meaning security investment alone (checkpoints, cameras, airstrikes, AUSSOM funding) cannot resolve the underlying problem.
insights.quote: Al-Shabaab has outlasted every campaign against it not because it is unbeatable, but because it has never had to face a unified opponent over time.
insights.locator: Somalia's Real Test

insights.claim: The real test facing Somalia this fall and winter is not whether the government can win a hypothetical 'final offensive,' but whether Mogadishu's political rivals and the federal member states can achieve reconciliation to deny al-Shabaab the space that infighting has historically given it, now with far less international support.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Sets the analytical benchmark for judging whether Somalia's current calm proves durable once AUSSOM's external scaffolding is pulled away.
insights.quote: It is whether Mogadishu’s political rivals and the country’s federal member states can find a path to political reconciliation to deny al-Shabaab the space that political infighting has given it.
insights.locator: The true test is also not whether
